source_text: His proluserim quasi de gradu primo adhuc et quasi de longinquo. sed exhinc iam ad certum et comminus dimicaturus, uideo aliquas etiamnunc lineas praeducendas, ad quas erit dimicandum, ad scripturas scilicet creatoris. secundum eas enim probaturus Christum creatoris fuisse, ut postea Christo suo adimpletas, necesse habeo ipsarum quoque scripturarum formam et, ut ita dixerim, naturam demandare, ne tunc in controuersiam deductae, cum adhibentur ad causas, et sua et causarum defensione commixta obtundant lectoris intentionem. duas itaque causas prophetici eloquii adlego agnoscendas abhinc aduersariis nostris: unam, qua futura interdum pro iam transactis enuntiantur. nam et diuinitati competit quaecumque decreuerit ut perfecta reputare, quia non sit apud illam differentia temporis, apud quam uniformen statum temporis dirigit aeternitas ipsa, et diuinationi propheticae magis familiare est id, quod prospiciat, dum prospicit, iam uisum atque ita iam expunctum. id est omni modo futurum, demonstrare, sicut per Esaiam: dorsum meum posui in flagella, maxillas autem meas in palmas, faciem meam uero non auerti a sputaminibus. siue enim Christus iam tunc in semetipsum, secundum nos, siue prophetes de semetipso, secundum Iudaeos, pronuntiabat, nondum tamen factum pro iam transacto sonabat. alia species erit, qua pleraque figurate portenduntur per aenigmata et allegorias et parabolas, aliter intellegenda quam scripta sunt nam et montes legimus destillaturos dulcorem, non tamen, ut sapam de petris aut defrutum de rupibus speres, et terram audimus lacte et melle manantem, (non tamen,) ut de glebis credas te umquam placentas et Samias coacturum, quia nec statim aquilicem et agricolam se deus repromisit dicens: ponam flumina in regione sitienti et in solitudine buxum et cedrum; sicut et praedicans de nationum conuersione: benedicent me bestiae agri, sirenes et filiae passerum, non utique ab hirundinum pullis et uulpeculis et illis monstruosis fabulosisque cantricibus fausta omina relaturus est. et quid ego de isto genere amplius? cum etiam haereticorum apostolus ipsam legem indulgentem bobus terentibus os liberum non de bobus, sed de nobis interpretetur, et petram, potui subministrando comitem, Christum adleget fuisse, docens proinde et Galatas duo argumenta filiorum Abrahae allegorice cucurrisse, et suggerens Ephesiis, quod in primordio de homine praedicatum est, relicturo patrem et matrem et futuris duobus in unam carnem, id se in Christum et ecclesiam agnoscere.
pass_a_gloss: I would have proceeded as if from the first step and as if from a distance, but from now on I will fight at close range and with certainty, and I see that some lines must be drawn beforehand, against which the battle will be fought, namely against the scriptures of the Creator. For according to them, I will prove that Christ was of the Creator, so that afterwards, having fulfilled his own Christ, I must also demand the form and, so to speak, the nature of those scriptures, lest they, when led into controversy and applied to causes, confuse the reader's intention with their own and the defense of the causes. Therefore, I adduce two reasons of prophetic speech to be recognized by our adversaries from now on: one, by which future events are sometimes announced as if they had already happened. For it is also fitting for divinity to consider whatever it has decreed as already perfect, because there is no difference of time with it, with which eternity itself directs a uniform state of time, and it is more familiar to prophetic divination to consider what it foresees as already seen and thus already fulfilled. This is to demonstrate in every way what is going to happen, as through Isaiah: I have put my back in whips, my cheeks in palms, and I have not turned my face away from spittings. For whether Christ was speaking about himself, according to us, or the prophet about himself, according to the Jews, it still sounded as if it had already been done, although it had not been done. There will be another kind, by which most things are foretold figuratively through enigmas and allegories and parables, to be understood differently than they are written. For we read that mountains will drip with sweetness, but you should not expect to suck sap from rocks or defrutum from cliffs, and we hear that the earth will flow with milk and honey, but you should not believe that you will ever make cakes and sweet breads from clods, because God did not immediately promise to be a bird-catcher and a farmer, saying: I will put rivers in a thirsty region and boxwood and cedar in a wilderness. And when predicting the conversion of nations, he says: the beasts of the field will bless me, the sirens and the daughters of the sparrow, but he will not certainly relate favorable omens from the young of swallows and foxes and those monstrous and fabulous singers. And what more can I say about this kind of thing? Since even the apostle of the heretics interprets the law itself, which indulges oxen that tread the grain, not about oxen, but about us, and he adds that the rock, which provided drink, was Christ, teaching thereby that the two arguments of the sons of Abraham ran allegorically, and suggesting to the Ephesians that what was predicted about man in the beginning, leaving father and mother and becoming one flesh, he recognizes as being about Christ and the church.
pass_b_english: I would have proceeded as if from a first step and from a distance, but from now on I will engage at close quarters and with certainty. I see that some lines must be drawn in advance, lines against which the battle will be joined—specifically, the scriptures of the Creator. I must establish the form and, so to speak, the nature of those scriptures now, because I intend to prove from them that Christ belonged to the Creator, and afterwards, having fulfilled his own Christ, I must not let those scriptures be dragged into controversy. If they are, their own defense and the defense of the causes will become entangled and blunt the reader's focus.

Therefore, I lay down two principles of prophetic speech for our adversaries to acknowledge from this point forward. The first: future events are sometimes announced as if they had already happened. This befits divinity, for whatever God decrees, he regards as already perfect; there is no difference of time with him, since eternity itself directs a uniform state of time. It is also more natural to prophetic divination to behold what it foresees as already seen and thus already accomplished. This demonstrates in every way that a thing is going to happen, just as through Isaiah: ‘I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to those who pull out the beard; I hid not my face from disgrace and spitting’ (Isaiah 50:6). Whether Christ spoke of himself, according to us, or the prophet spoke of himself, according to the Jews, the utterance sounded as though the deed were already done, though it had not yet been done.

The second principle: most things are foretold figuratively, through enigmas, allegories, and parables, to be understood differently than they are written. We read that mountains will drip sweetness, yet you should not expect to suck sap from rocks or syrup from cliffs. We hear that the earth will flow with milk and honey, yet you should not believe you will ever bake cakes and sweet breads from clods of earth. God did not promise to become a bird-catcher and a farmer outright, saying: ‘I will put rivers in a thirsty land, and cedar and boxwood in a wilderness’ (Isaiah 41:18-19). And when predicting the conversion of the nations, he says: ‘The beasts of the field will honor me, the jackals and the ostriches’ (Isaiah 43:20). He will certainly not derive favorable omens from the young of swallows, foxes, and those monstrous and fabulous singers.

What more need I say of this kind? Even the apostle of the heretics interprets the law that indulges oxen treading out the grain—not concerning oxen, but concerning us (1 Corinthians 9:9-10). He adds that the rock which supplied drink was Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4). He thereby teaches that the two lines of Abraham's sons ran their course allegorically (Galatians 4:22-24). And he suggests to the Ephesians that what was predicted of man in the beginning—that he shall leave father and mother and the two shall become one flesh—he recognizes as referring to Christ and the church (Ephesians 5:31-32).

review.notes: Pass B introduces significant deviations from the Locked Latin in the translation of specific biblical allusions/quotes. 1. For the Isaiah 50:6 allusion: Latin 'maxillas autem meas in palmas' (my cheeks in palms) is rendered in Pass B as 'my cheeks to those who pull out the beard', which is a significant departure from the source text. 2. For the Isaiah 43:20 allusion: Latin 'sirenes et filiae passerum' (sirens and daughters of the sparrow) is rendered in Pass B as 'the jackals and the ostriches', which is a complete substitution of the text. 3. For the Galatians allusion: Latin 'Galatas duo argumenta filiorum Abrahae' (two arguments of the sons of Abraham) is rendered in Pass B as 'the two lines of Abraham's sons ran their course', which alters the sense of the argument being discussed.
reasons: Pass B fails scripture fidelity: 'maxillas autem meas in palmas' is translated as 'my cheeks to those who pull out the beard'; 'sirenes et filiae passerum' is translated as 'the jackals and the ostriches'; 'Galatas duo argumenta filiorum Abrahae' is translated as 'the two lines of Abraham's sons ran their course'.
